G0A01: RF is non-ionizing. Its effect on the body is heating, like a microwave oven, not radiation poisoning.
G0A02: Exposure depends on power density, frequency (the body absorbs some frequencies more) and duty cycle (how much of the time you transmit). All of them count.
G0A03: You can show compliance by calculation from OET Bulletin 65, by computer modeling, or by measuring with calibrated equipment. All three work.
G0A04: Time averaging = total exposure averaged over a set period (6 minutes controlled, 30 minutes uncontrolled), so short bursts count less than steady carriers.
G0A05: If you exceed the limits you must stop people from being exposed: move the antenna, cut power, or keep people out of the area.
G0A06: No exemption means you must do a full RF exposure evaluation, and the FCC method is OET Bulletin 65.
G0A07: Lower duty cycle = less time on the air, so the average exposure is lower and you can run more power for the same exposure.
G0A08: Do a routine RF exposure evaluation, then keep people out of any high-exposure spots it finds.
G0A09: Field strength needs a calibrated field strength meter with a calibrated antenna. SWR meters and scopes do not measure the field in the air.
G0A10: The fix is to keep the beam from pointing at the neighbor when they are there. Changing antennas does not solve the main-lobe problem.
G0A11: Indoors, people are close to the antenna, so make sure occupied areas stay under the MPE limits.
G0A12: The RF exposure rules cover every station that averages more than one milliwatt. Amateurs are not exempt.
G0B01: Fuses and breakers go only in the hot wires. Never fuse the neutral or the ground; opening them would leave the hots live.
G0B02: A 20 amp breaker needs at least AWG 12 wire. Remember: 14 gauge = 15 amps, 12 gauge = 20 amps.
G0B03: AWG 14 wire is rated for 15 amps, so use a 15 amp fuse or breaker. A bigger breaker lets the wire overheat.
G0B04: The lightning ground goes outside the building, so the strike's current never comes indoors.
G0B05: A GFCI trips when current leaks from a hot wire straight to ground (maybe through you). Hot to neutral is normal load current.
G0B06: The National Electrical Code covers electrical safety: wiring, grounding, breakers. It says nothing about RF exposure or bandwidth.
G0B07: A harness must be rated for the climber's weight and still within its service life. An expired or overloaded harness can fail.
G0B08: Lock out and tag every circuit that powers devices on the tower before climbing, so no one can switch it on while you are up there.
G0B09: Generators make carbon monoxide, so run them only in a well-ventilated area, never indoors.
G0B10: The danger of lead solder is lead on your hands getting into food. Wash after soldering.
G0B11: All ground rods must be bonded together with the station's other grounds, so lightning cannot create a voltage difference between them.
G0B12: An interlock cuts the dangerous voltage when the cabinet is opened, so you cannot touch it by accident.
G0B13: Arrestors go where the feed lines enter the building, so a surge is sent to ground before it comes inside.
G1A01: General can't use all of 80, 40, 20 and 15 meters: each has an Extra-only slice at the bottom. Same four bands as G1A08.
G1A02: 30 meters is CW and data only. No phone at all.
G1A03: 30 meters is narrow (50 kHz) and limited to CW and data, so no images either.
G1A05: 7.125 to 7.175 MHz is the Extra-only part of the 40 meter phone segment. General phone on 40 starts at 7.175.
G1A06: Secondary means you must not interfere with the primary users and must accept their interference.
G1A07: CW is allowed everywhere on every amateur band, so General can send CW across the entire 10 meter band.
G1A08: 80, 40, 20 and 15 meters each have a bottom slice only Extras can use.
G1A09: 15 meters runs 21.000 to 21.450 MHz, and General phone is 21.275 to 21.450, so 21300 kHz = 21.300 MHz fits. The other choices are on 20, 17 and 12 meters.
G1A10: 10 meter repeaters live above 29.5 MHz, near the top of the band.
G1A11: Extras get the bottom of each phone segment, so General gets the upper part.
G1B01: Up to 200 feet you need no FAA notice or FCC registration (unless you are near a public-use airport).
G1B02: Only one beacon per band from the same location.
G1B03: Beacons exist so hams can observe propagation and reception.
G1B04: Occasionally relaying US government weather and propagation forecasts is allowed. Unidentified tests and encryption are not.
G1B05: One-way Morse code practice transmissions are allowed. Unidentified tests and sales ads are not.
G1B06: PRB-1: local rules must reasonably accommodate amateur antennas and be the minimum needed for a legitimate local purpose.
G1B07: Abbreviations and procedural signals are fine as long as they don't hide the meaning of the message.
G1B08: You can work any country unless its government has told the ITU it objects to contacts with US amateurs.
G1B09: Automatic beacons on HF are allowed only from 28.20 to 28.30 MHz on 10 meters.
G1B10: A beacon may run up to 100 watts PEP output.
G1B11: The FCC decides what good engineering and good amateur practice means where Part 97 is silent.
G1C01: 10.140 MHz is on 30 meters, where the limit is 200 watts PEP output.
G1C02: 12 meters has the normal amateur limit: 1500 watts PEP output.
G1C03: On 60 meters USB channels, the limit is 2.8 kHz bandwidth.
G1C04: On 60 meters, if your antenna is not a dipole you must keep a record of its gain (power is set as ERP relative to a dipole).
G1C05: General gets the full 1500 watts PEP output on 10 meters (28 MHz).
G1C06: 160 meters (1.8 MHz) allows the full 1500 watts PEP output.
G1C07: A new digital code is legal once its technical characteristics are publicly documented, so others can decode it.
G1C11: Power limits are measured as PEP output from the transmitter.
G1D01: If you once held a General, Advanced or Extra license that was not revoked, you get credit for those elements (you still pass Element 2).
G1D02: A General class VE can give only the Technician exam.
G1D03: With a valid CSCE for General you may use all General and Technician privileges right away, before the database updates.
G1D04: Every exam session needs at least three VEs of General class or higher for a Technician exam.
G1D05: Running a US station remotely from abroad needs only your US operator/primary station license.
G1D06: Until the upgrade shows in the database, add AG whenever you use General privileges.
G1D07: A Volunteer Examiner Coordinator (VEC) accredits VEs, not the FCC directly.
G1D08: A non-citizen can be a VE if they hold an FCC amateur license of General or higher.
G1D09: A CSCE is good for 365 days of element credit.
G1D10: VEs must be at least 18 years old.
G1D11: After the 2-year grace period, show proof of the expired license and pass the current Element 2 (Technician) exam to get it back.
G1D12: You are using a station in another country, so that country's rules apply, not the FCC's.
G1E01: A third party whose amateur license was revoked and not reinstated cannot take part. Citizenship and language don't matter.
G1E02: A 10 meter repeater can relay a Technician's 2 meter signal only if the 10 meter repeater's control operator is General or higher.
G1E03: To reach an automatic digital station outside the auto segments, the station starting the contact must be under local or remote control.
G1E04: Near an FCC monitoring station, on a band where amateurs are secondary, or running spread spectrum: all need care to avoid harmful interference.
G1E05: With a third-party agreement, messages must be about amateur radio, personal remarks, or emergencies and disaster relief.
G1E06: North and South America are ITU Region 2.
G1E07: Amateur stations may not talk to unlicensed Wi-Fi stations anywhere in 2.4 GHz.
G1E08: Spread spectrum is limited to 10 watts PEP output.
G1E10: Those five frequencies (14.100, 18.110, 21.150, 24.930, 28.200 MHz) are the international propagation beacon network.
G1E11: Automatic digital stations may talk to each other anywhere on 6 meters and up, and in limited segments of some HF bands.
G1E12: Remote control changes nothing: third-party messages are fine whenever the rules otherwise allow them.
G2A01: Convention: 14 MHz (20 meters) and up use upper sideband.
G2A02: Convention: 160, 75 and 40 meters (below 10 MHz) use lower sideband.
G2A03: VHF and UHF are above 14 MHz, so SSB there is upper sideband.
G2A04: 17 and 12 meters are above 14 MHz, so upper sideband.
G2A05: Single sideband is the standard HF voice mode: narrow and efficient.
G2A06: SSB sends no carrier and only one sideband: less bandwidth, and all the power goes into the part that carries your voice.
G2A07: SSB = one sideband only. The carrier and the other sideband are both suppressed.
G2A08: To break in on a phone contact, say your call sign once, then wait.
G2A09: LSB on the low bands is simply custom. Neither sideband is more efficient or more legal.
G2A10: VOX keys the transmitter when you talk, so your hands are free. It changes nothing about the signal.
G2A11: CQ DX from the lower 48 means the caller wants stations outside the lower 48 states.
G2A12: ALC responds to how hard you drive the transmitter, so set it with the mic gain (transmit audio).
G2B01: No one owns a frequency. Only emergency traffic gets priority.
G2B02: A distress call comes first: acknowledge the station and find out what help is needed.
G2B03: When propagation shifts and stations overlap, work it out politely with them. No one has priority.
G2B04: CW signals are narrow, so 150 to 500 Hz of separation is enough.
G2B05: SSB is about 3 kHz wide, so give 2 to 3 kHz of separation.
G2B06: Ask first: QRL? on CW, or is this frequency in use? on phone, followed by your call sign.
G2B07: Follow the voluntary band plan when picking a frequency to call on.
G2B08: 50.100 to 50.125 MHz is the 6 meter DX window: stations in the lower 48 use it only to work stations outside the lower 48.
G2B09: RACES stations must have a licensed amateur as control operator. A government official without a license cannot be one.
G2B10: A backup frequency keeps the net going when interference or conditions hit.
G2B11: RACES drills may run up to 1 hour per week without special authorization.
G2C01: QSK (full break-in) lets you hear between the dots and dashes you send.
G2C02: QRS? = please send slower. So slow down.
G2C03: KN = go ahead, but only the station I am working. Others please don't call.
G2C04: QRL? = is this frequency in use? (or are you busy?)
G2C05: Answer at a speed you can copy, but not faster than the CQ was sent.
G2C06: Zero beat = setting your transmit frequency exactly on the station you hear.
G2C07: A C after the RST report means the signal is chirpy (its frequency wobbles).
G2C08: AR marks the end of a formal message. SK ends the contact.
G2C09: QSL = I have received and understood.
G2C10: QRN = I am troubled by static (natural noise). QRM is man-made interference.
G2C11: QRV = I am ready to receive.
G2D01: Volunteer Monitors are amateurs formally enlisted to watch the bands for rule violations.
G2D02: The program's goal is to get hams to police themselves and follow the rules.
G2D03: Monitors find a station by comparing beam headings from their different homes and seeing where the lines cross.
G2D04: An azimuthal map is centered on one place and shows true bearings and distances from there, so you know where to point your beam.
G2D05: A general call: say CQ a few times, this is, your call sign a few times, then listen. Repeat as needed.
G2D06: Long path is the other way around the Earth: 180 degrees from the short-path heading.
G2D07: NATO phonetics: Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta. The others are old or made-up alphabets.
G2D08: Logs are no longer required, but they help if the FCC asks about your station.
G2D09: In a contest you must still identify by the normal FCC rules. Sending in a log or QSL cards is optional.
G2D10: QRP = low power operation (5 watts or less for CW by custom).
G2D11: Early signal reports let each station adjust to the conditions (power, speed, mode).
G2E01: RTTY via AFSK is sent on LSB by convention.
G2E02: VARA is a digital protocol used to send Winlink email.
G2E03: Interference to PACTOR or VARA shows up as retries, timeouts, long pauses and failed connections. All of these.
G2E04: FT8 stations take turns in 15 second slots. Answer on a clear spot in the opposite slot from the station you call.
G2E05: JT65, JT9, FT4 and FT8 all use upper sideband.
G2E06: Standard amateur RTTY shift is 170 Hz between mark and space.
G2E07: FT8 timing slots demand your computer clock be right to within about 1 second.
G2E08: On 20 meters, digital modes cluster from 14.070 to 14.100 MHz.
G2E09: PACTOR is a link between exactly two stations. A third station can't join.
G2E10: To reach a gateway, send a connect request on its published frequency.
G2E11: AREDN mesh networks carry high-speed data during emergencies and community events.
G2E12: Winlink is radio email, it can run over packet, and it works on both VHF and HF. All three.
G2E13: A Winlink Remote Message Server is called a gateway.
G2E14: Mark and space reversed, the wrong baud rate, or the wrong sideband can each stop an RTTY decode. All of these.
G2E15: On 20 meters, FT8 sits around 14.074 to 14.077 MHz.
G3A01: More sunspots = more ionizing radiation = a denser ionosphere, so the higher HF bands open more often.
G3A02: A sudden ionospheric disturbance thickens the D region, which absorbs lower frequencies most. Higher bands get through better.
G3A03: Flare radiation travels at the speed of light, so it reaches Earth in about 8 minutes.
G3A04: With few sunspots, the ionosphere is too thin to bend the high bands back: 15, 12 and 10 meters are the least reliable.
G3A05: Solar flux is the Sun's radio noise measured at a wavelength of 10.7 cm (2800 MHz). Higher flux = better high-band conditions.
G3A06: A geomagnetic storm is a temporary disturbance of Earth's magnetic field, usually from a CME or solar wind stream.
G3A07: 20 meters is the dependable band: it supports worldwide daytime contacts at any point in the solar cycle.
G3A08: Geomagnetic storms hit the polar regions hardest, so high-latitude HF paths degrade.
G3A09: Storms make auroras, and auroras can reflect VHF signals.
G3A10: The Sun turns once about every 27 days, so active regions come back around on a 26 to 28 day cycle.
G3A11: A CME is a cloud of particles, much slower than light: 15 hours to several days to arrive.
G3A12: K-index = short-term (3-hour) stability of Earth's magnetic field. K for quicK.
G3A13: A-index = long-term (daily average) stability of Earth's magnetic field.
G3A14: Coronal hole particles disturb Earth's magnetic field, and that disturbs HF.
G3B01: Long path takes a longer route around the Earth and arrives a moment later, so you may hear a slight echo.
G3B02: MUF depends on path distance and location, time of day and season, and solar radiation and disturbances. All of these.
G3B03: Just below the MUF: the highest frequency that still comes back, and higher frequencies are absorbed less.
G3B04: Automated receiving networks on the internet show where your signal is actually being heard.
G3B05: Between the LUF and MUF is the usable window: those signals are refracted back to Earth.
G3B06: Below the LUF, signals are absorbed (mostly by the D region) before they reach the other station.
G3B07: LUF = Lowest Usable Frequency between two specific points.
G3B08: MUF = Maximum Usable Frequency between two points.
G3B09: One F2 hop covers up to about 2,500 miles, because F2 is the highest region.
G3B10: One E region hop covers up to about 1,200 miles. E is lower than F2, so shorter hops.
G3B11: If the LUF is above the MUF, there is no usable window: no ordinary skywave on that path.
G3B12: Summer thunderstorms make lots of static on the lower HF bands.
G3C01: From the ground up: D, E, F1, F2. D is closest to Earth.
G3C02: Critical frequency = the highest frequency that still gets refracted back at that angle.
G3C03: F2 is the highest region, so the bounce comes down farthest away.
G3C04: Critical angle = the highest takeoff angle that still comes back. Aim any steeper and the signal goes through.
G3C05: In daylight the D region forms and absorbs the low bands (160 to 40 meters), so long distance on them waits for night.
G3C06: Scatter signals arrive over many paths at once, so they sound fluttery.
G3C07: Scatter energy reaches you by several different paths at once, which distorts it.
G3C08: Only a small part of the energy gets scattered into the skip zone, so the signals are weak.
G3C09: Scatter lets you hear stations in your skip zone (too far for ground wave, too close for skywave).
G3C10: NVIS = short-range HF sent nearly straight up (high angle) and reflected straight back down.
G3C11: The D region absorbs signals below about 10 MHz during the day.
G4A01: A notch filter cuts a narrow slot to remove a steady carrier (a whistle) from the receiver passband.
G4A02: Switching CW to the other sideband moves interfering signals to the other side of your filter, so you may lose them.
G4A03: A noise blanker turns the receiver gain down for the instant of each noise pulse.
G4A04: Tune the plate for a pronounced dip in plate current: that is resonance.
G4A05: ALC holds back the drive so the amplifier isn't overdriven.
G4A06: A tuner matches the transmitter to the feed line, increasing the power transferred. It does not lower the SWR on the feed line itself.
G4A07: Too much noise reduction starts to distort the signals you want.
G4A08: Adjust LOAD for the power you want without exceeding the maximum plate current.
G4A09: The delay gives the amplifier's relay time to switch the antenna before RF arrives.
G4A10: An electronic keyer makes the dots and dashes automatically from paddle presses.
G4A11: ALC action distorts AFSK data signals, so set the audio so ALC stays inactive.
G4A12: Dual VFOs let you transmit on one frequency and listen on another (working split).
G4A13: An attenuator cuts very strong signals before they overload the receiver.
G4B01: Horizontal and vertical amplifiers move the trace on an oscilloscope.
G4B02: A scope shows the whole waveform, so it can measure complex waveforms a voltmeter can't.
G4B03: To see the keying waveform (its rise and fall), use an oscilloscope.
G4B04: Feed the attenuated RF output of the transmitter to the scope's vertical input to see the envelope.
G4B05: High input impedance draws almost no current, so the meter barely loads the circuit it measures.
G4B06: A digital multimeter reads with higher precision than an analog meter.
G4B07: A two-tone test uses two audio tones that are not harmonically related.
G4B08: A two-tone test checks linearity: how cleanly the transmitter amplifies.
G4B09: A moving needle is easier to watch when you're tuning for a peak or a dip.
G4B10: A directional wattmeter reads forward and reflected power, which gives you the SWR.
G4B11: An antenna analyzer measures SWR of the antenna and feed line connected to it. No transmitter needed.
G4B12: Strong nearby signals put received power into the analyzer and spoil its SWR readings.
G4B13: An antenna analyzer can measure the impedance of coax.
G4C01: A bypass capacitor shunts RF to ground while letting audio through.
G4C02: Arcing at a poor connection makes noise across a wide range of frequencies.
G4C03: SSB interference to audio gear sounds like distorted speech.
G4C04: CW interference to audio gear sounds like on-and-off humming or clicking, keyed with your sending.
G4C05: A ground wire can have high impedance at your frequency (for example, near a quarter wavelength long), so RF voltage builds up at the station end.
G4C06: A resonant ground wire puts high RF voltage on your equipment cases.
G4C07: A lightning strike's heat would melt a soldered joint. Use mechanical or welded connections.
G4C08: A ferrite choke on the cable blocks common-mode RF on its outside.
G4C09: Bond all enclosures together so there's no voltage difference to drive a loop current.
G4C10: A ground loop in audio wiring shows up as hum on your transmitted signal.
G4C11: Bonding all enclosures together keeps them at the same RF potential, so no hot spots.
G4C12: Grounding the chassis makes sure a fault can't leave dangerous voltage on the metal case.
G4D01: A speech processor makes your voice sound louder (more punch) without raising peak power.
G4D02: It raises the average power. Peak power stays the same.
G4D03: A badly set processor gives distortion, splatter (intermod) and lots of background noise. All of these.
G4D04: An S meter shows received signal strength.
G4D06: One S unit is about 6 dB.
G4D07: S8 to S9 is one S unit, 6 dB, about 4 times the power (3 dB = 2x, so 6 dB = 2 x 2).
G4D08: LSB lies below the displayed carrier: 7.178 - 0.003 = 7.175, so 7.175 to 7.178 MHz.
G4D09: USB lies above the displayed carrier: 14.347 + 0.003 = 14.350, so 14.347 to 14.350 MHz.
G4D10: LSB extends 3 kHz below the dial, so stay at least 3 kHz above the lower edge.
G4D11: USB extends 3 kHz above the dial, so stay at least 3 kHz below the upper edge.
G4E01: A capacitance hat adds capacitance at the top, making a short antenna act electrically longer.
G4E02: A corona ball rounds the tip so high RF voltage doesn't discharge into the air.
G4E03: Wire a 100 watt mobile straight to the battery with heavy wire (fused).
G4E04: A cigarette lighter socket's wiring is too light for the current a 100 watt rig draws.
G4E05: The biggest limit on HF mobile is the poor efficiency of the electrically short antenna.
G4E06: Shortened antennas have high Q, so their usable bandwidth is very narrow.
G4E07: Charging system, fuel system and control computers can all make noise in a car. All of these.
G4E08: Solar cells are wired series-parallel: series for voltage, parallel for current.
G4E09: A silicon solar cell gives about 0.5 volts open circuit.
G4E10: The series diode stops the battery from discharging back through the panel at night.
G4E11: A lithium iron phosphate battery needs a charge controller between it and the panel.
G5A01: In a series LC circuit at resonance the two reactances cancel, leaving only resistance, so impedance is very low.
G5A02: Reactance is the opposition to AC caused by capacitance or inductance. Resistance is the DC-style opposition.
G5A03: An inductor opposes AC with reactance.
G5A04: A capacitor opposes AC with reactance too.
G5A05: Inductive reactance rises with frequency: XL = 2 pi f L.
G5A06: Capacitive reactance falls as frequency rises: XC = 1 / (2 pi f C).
G5A07: Admittance is the inverse of impedance (1/Z). Conductance is the inverse of resistance.
G5A08: Impedance = voltage divided by current (Z = E / I), like Ohm's law for AC.
G5A09: Reactance is an opposition to current, so it is measured in ohms.
G5A10: Transformers, pi-networks and lengths of transmission line can all match impedances at RF. All of these.
G5A11: Reactance is X (XL for inductors, XC for capacitors). Z is impedance.
G5A12: At resonance XL equals XC, and because they act in opposite directions they cancel.
G5B02: In parallel, the total current is the sum of the branch currents.
G5B04: P = E x I = 12 x 0.2 = 2.4 watts.
G5B05: P = I squared x R = 0.007 x 0.007 x 1,250 = 0.061 watts, about 61 milliwatts.
G5B06: 200 V peak-to-peak = 100 V peak. RMS = 100 x 0.707 = 70.7 V. PEP = 70.7 x 70.7 / 50 = 100 watts.
G5B07: RMS is defined as the AC value that heats a resistor the same as that much DC.
G5B08: Peak = 120 x 1.414 = 169.7 V. Peak-to-peak is twice that: 339.4 volts.
G5B10: 1 dB down leaves 10 to the power -0.1 = 0.794 of the power, so 1 - 0.794 = 20.6 percent is lost.
G5B11: An unmodulated carrier is steady, so its peak power equals its average power: ratio 1.00.
G5B12: E = square root of (P x R) = square root of (1200 x 50) = square root of 60,000 = 245 volts.
G5B13: Unmodulated carrier: PEP equals average power, so 1060 watts.
G5B14: 500 V peak-to-peak = 250 V peak. RMS = 250 x 0.707 = 176.8 V. PEP = 176.8 x 176.8 / 50 = 625 watts.
G5C01: The changing magnetic field of the primary links to the secondary: mutual inductance.
G5C02: Run backward, a 4:1 step-down becomes a 1:4 step-up, so the voltage is multiplied by 4.
G5C05: Stepping voltage up steps current down, so the primary carries more current and needs thicker wire.
G5C06: Turns ratio 1500 / 500 = 3, so 120 V x 3 = 360 volts.
G5C07: Turns ratio = square root of the impedance ratio = square root of (600 / 50) = square root of 12 = 3.5 to 1.
G5C08: Capacitors in parallel add: 5.0 + 5.0 + 0.75 nF (750 pF) = 10.750 nanofarads.
G5C09: Equal capacitors in series: divide by how many. 100 / 3 = 33.3 microfarads.
G5C10: Equal inductors in parallel: divide by how many. 10 / 3 = 3.3 millihenries.
G5C11: Inductors in series add, like resistors: 20 + 50 = 70 millihenries.
G5C12: Capacitors in series combine like parallel resistors: (20 x 50) / (20 + 50) = 1000 / 70 = 14.3 microfarads.
G5C13: Capacitors add in parallel, so add a capacitor in parallel to increase capacitance.
G5C14: Inductors add in series, so add an inductor in series to increase inductance.
G6A01: Don't discharge a 12 volt lead-acid battery below 10.5 volts if you want it to last.
G6A02: Low internal resistance means the battery can deliver high current.
G6A03: Germanium diodes turn on at about 0.3 volts.
G6A04: Electrolytics pack a lot of capacitance into a small size.
G6A05: Silicon diodes turn on at about 0.7 volts.
G6A06: A wire-wound resistor is a coil, so its inductance upsets RF circuits.
G6A07: As a switch, a transistor sits at saturation (fully on) or cutoff (fully off).
G6A08: Low voltage ceramic capacitors are cheap.
G6A09: In a MOSFET, a thin insulating layer separates the gate from the channel (metal-oxide).
G6A10: The control grid sits between cathode and plate and controls the flow of electrons.
G6A11: Above its self-resonant frequency, an inductor's stray capacitance takes over and it acts like a capacitor.
G6A12: The screen grid cuts the capacitance between the control grid and the plate.
G6B01: A ferrite's mix (the material blend) decides which frequencies it works best at.
G6B03: CMOS uses far less power than TTL.
G6B04: BNC connectors are good to about 4 GHz.
G6B05: Ferrite toroids give large inductance, can be tuned for a frequency range, and hold the field inside the core. All of these.
G6B06: An op amp is an analog device.
G6B07: Type N connectors are moisture resistant and good to 10 GHz.
G6B08: An LED lights when forward biased.
G6B10: A ferrite bead adds impedance in the path of common-mode current on the outside of the shield.
G6B11: SMA is a small threaded connector good to several GHz.
G6B12: RCA phono plugs are used for audio and low frequency or DC connections.
G7A01: A bleeder resistor drains the filter capacitors after power is off, so they can't shock you.
G7A02: A power supply filter uses capacitors and inductors to smooth the pulses into steady DC.
G7A03: Two diodes with a center-tapped transformer = full-wave. A bridge uses four diodes and no center tap.
G7A04: A half-wave rectifier needs only one diode.
G7A05: Half-wave passes only one half of each cycle: 180 degrees.
G7A06: Full-wave uses both halves of the cycle: all 360 degrees.
G7A07: Full-wave flips every negative half up, so you get DC pulses at twice the AC frequency.
G7A08: A switchmode supply runs at high frequency, so its transformer and filter parts can be much smaller.
G7A09: Symbol 1 is the FET: a straight channel line with the gate on one side.
G7A10: Symbol 5 is the Zener diode: a diode whose bar has bent ends.
G7A11: Symbol 2 is the NPN transistor: the emitter arrow points out (Not Pointing iN).
G7A12: Symbol 6 is the solid core transformer: two coils with straight lines between them for the iron core.
G7A13: Symbol 7 is the tapped inductor: one coil with a connection coming off its middle.
G7B01: Neutralizing cancels the feedback that makes an amplifier oscillate on its own.
G7B02: Class C conducts for the smallest part of each cycle, so it wastes the least power: highest efficiency.
G7B03: AND: the output is high only when both inputs are high.
G7B04: Class A conducts the whole cycle: 100% of the time.
G7B05: Each bit has 2 states, so 3 bits = 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 states.
G7B06: A shift register moves data one step along a row of circuits on each clock pulse.
G7B07: An oscillator is an amplifier with a filter feeding part of its output back to its input.
G7B08: Efficiency = RF power out divided by DC power in.
G7B09: An LC oscillator's frequency is set by the inductance and capacitance of its tank circuit.
G7B10: Linear = the output is a faithful, bigger copy of the input waveform.
G7B11: FM keeps a constant amplitude, so a non-linear Class C stage can amplify it. SSB and AM need linear amps.
G7C01: The balanced modulator makes both sidebands; a filter picks the one you want.
G7C02: A balanced modulator outputs double-sideband RF with the carrier suppressed.
G7C03: A matching transformer makes the transmitter and the feed line see the impedance they want.
G7C04: A product detector recovers the audio from a single sideband signal in the receiver.
G7C05: A DDS tunes over a wide range digitally while keeping crystal-oscillator stability.
G7C06: DSP filters are software, so you can create almost any bandwidth and shape.
G7C07: Insertion loss is how much a filter attenuates signals inside its passband.
G7C08: Front-end gain, demodulator bandwidth and front-end noise figure all affect sensitivity. All of these.
G7C09: I and Q are the same signal 90 degrees apart (in phase and quadrature).
G7C10: With I and Q, software can create or decode any type of modulation.
G7C11: In an SDR, software does filtering, detection and modulation. All of these.
G7C12: Cutoff frequency: where output falls to half power (3 dB down).
G7C13: Ultimate rejection is the best a filter can reject signals outside its passband.
G7C14: Bandwidth is measured between the upper and lower half-power (3 dB) points.
G8A01: Direct FSK changes the oscillator's frequency directly with the digital signal.
G8A02: Changing the phase angle to carry information is phase modulation.
G8A03: Changing the instantaneous frequency to carry information is frequency modulation.
G8A04: A reactance modulator on an amplifier stage shifts the phase, so the result is phase modulation.
G8A05: Amplitude modulation varies the instantaneous power level of the RF.
G8A06: QPSK31 is sideband sensitive, has error correction, and uses about the same bandwidth as BPSK31. All of these.
G8A07: Single sideband sends just one sideband with no carrier, so it is the narrowest phone mode.
G8A08: Overmodulation distorts the signal and spreads it out: excessive bandwidth (splatter).
G8A10: Flat-topping is the peaks clipped flat by too much drive or speech level.
G8A11: The modulation envelope is the outline you get by connecting the peaks of the modulated RF.
G8A12: QPSK sends two bits at a time using four phases: 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees.
G8A13: Link budget = transmit power plus antenna gains minus all losses, as seen at the receiver.
G8A14: Link margin = received power minus the minimum signal the receiver needs.
G8B01: You tune the local oscillator so each received signal mixes down to the same IF.
G8B02: An image is a signal twice the IF away from the one you want; it mixes to the same IF.
G8B03: Mixing two RF signals is heterodyning.
G8B04: A multiplier stage makes a harmonic to reach the final frequency in a VHF FM transmitter.
G8B05: Odd-order products (like 2F1 - F2) land right next to the original signals.
G8B06: Carson's rule: 2 x (deviation + audio) = 2 x (5 + 3) = 16 kHz.
G8B07: Multiplication: 146.52 / 12.21 = 12. Deviation is multiplied too, so the oscillator needs 5 kHz / 12 = 416.7 Hz.
G8B08: High duty cycle modes (FM, RTTY, FT8) can run the transmitter over its average power rating.
G8B09: Matching receiver bandwidth to the mode lets in the signal but as little noise as possible: best signal-to-noise ratio.
G8B10: Faster symbol rates need wider bandwidth.
G8B11: A mixer outputs the sum and the difference of its two input frequencies.
G8B12: Intermodulation: two signals mixing in a non-linear circuit to make unwanted outputs.
G8B13: Odd-order = the multipliers add to an odd number. 2F1 - F2: 2 + 1 = 3, odd.
G8C02: WSPR is a very low power beacon mode for checking HF propagation.
G8C03: A packet's header carries the routing and handling information.
G8C04: Baudot is a 5-bit code with start and stop bits added (used for RTTY).
G8C05: NAK = not acknowledged: please send that packet again.
G8C06: After too many failed tries, ARQ gives up and drops the connection.
G8C07: FT8 decodes signals far below the noise, at very low signal-to-noise ratios.
G8C08: Varicode gives common lowercase letters short codes, so uppercase letters take longer to send.
G8C09: In a mesh, if one node fails, packets can route through another node.
G8C10: FEC sends extra redundant data, so the receiver can rebuild what was lost.
G8C11: The two FSK frequencies are called mark and space.
G8C13: Vertical lines either side of a data signal on a waterfall mean overmodulation (splatter).
G8C14: Waterfall: frequency across, time running down, signal strength as brightness or color.
G8C15: FT8 reports are signal-to-noise in a 2.5 kHz bandwidth: +3 means 3 dB above the noise.
G8C16: DMR, D-STAR and System Fusion are the digital voice modes.
G9A01: Parallel line impedance is set by how far apart the wires are and how thick they are. Length and frequency don't change it.
G9A02: High SWR makes power travel the line more than once, so a lossy line loses more.
G9A04: Power reflects when the feed line impedance and the antenna feed point impedance differ.
G9A05: Coax loss goes up as frequency goes up.
G9A06: Feed line loss is given in decibels per 100 feet.
G9A07: No standing waves means the antenna's feed point impedance matches the feed line's characteristic impedance.
G9A08: A tuner at the transmitter only fixes what the transmitter sees. The feed line still runs at 5:1.
G9A09: SWR = bigger impedance over smaller: 200 / 50 = 4, so 4:1.
G9A11: A lossy line eats some of the reflected power before it gets back, so SWR at the input looks lower (better) than it really is.
G9B01: A random wire fed right at the rig puts RF current on the station equipment, which becomes part of the antenna.
G9B02: Sloping the radials downward raises a ground plane's feed point impedance toward 50 ohms.
G9B03: A vertical ground plane radiates equally in all compass directions: omnidirectional in azimuth.
G9B04: A dipole radiates broadside: a figure-eight at right angles to the wire, with nulls off the ends.
G9B05: A dipole less than 1/2 wavelength high sends most energy upward, so at high angles its pattern is almost omnidirectional.
G9B06: Ground radials go on the surface or just a few inches under it.
G9B07: As a dipole gets closer to the ground, its feed point impedance steadily drops.
G9B08: Moving the feed point from the center toward the end raises the impedance steadily (current falls, voltage rises).
G9B09: Horizontal antennas have lower ground losses than verticals, which need a good ground system.
G9B10: Half wave in feet = 468 / MHz = 468 / 14.25 = 32.8, about 33 feet.
G9B11: Half wave in feet = 468 / MHz = 468 / 3.55 = 131.8, about 132 feet.
G9B12: Quarter wave in feet = 234 / MHz = 234 / 28.5 = 8.2, about 8 feet.
G9C01: Larger-diameter elements widen a Yagi's bandwidth.
G9C02: The driven element is about 1/2 wavelength, like a dipole.
G9C03: Reflector longer, director shorter than the driven element.
G9C04: dBi compares to an isotropic source, dBd to a dipole. A dipole has 2.15 dBi, so dBi is 2.15 dB higher.
G9C05: A longer boom with more directors gives more gain.
G9C07: Front-to-back = power in the main lobe compared with power off the back.
G9C08: The main lobe is the direction of strongest radiation.
G9C09: Two stacked Yagis double the gain: about 3 dB more.
G9C10: Boom length, number of elements and element spacing all tune gain, front-to-back and SWR bandwidth. All of these.
G9C11: A beta or hairpin match is a shorted stub of line across the Yagi feed point to match its impedance.
G9C12: A gamma match attaches at the element's center, which is at zero voltage, so the element needn't be insulated from the boom.
G9D01: For NVIS, mount a horizontal dipole low, between 1/10 and 1/4 wavelength high, so it sends energy straight up.
G9D02: An end-fed half wave is fed at the end, where voltage is high and current low: very high impedance.
G9D03: A halo radiates equally around itself in the plane of the halo (like a horizontal omni).
G9D04: Traps switch sections of the antenna in and out by frequency, giving multiband operation.
G9D05: Stacking Yagis one above another narrows the main lobe in elevation (a lower, flatter beam).
G9D06: A log-periodic's big advantage is wide bandwidth.
G9D07: In a log-periodic, element length and spacing change logarithmically along the boom.
G9D08: A screwdriver antenna runs a motor to change its base loading coil's inductance.
G9D09: A Beverage is a long, low wire for directional receiving on MF and low HF.
G9D10: A small loop has its nulls broadside to the loop (at right angles to its plane).
G9D11: Multiband antennas resonate on many frequencies, so they reject harmonics poorly.
G9D12: A dipole hung from one center support with the ends drooping is an inverted V.
